section.title: Paul's Change of Plans
section.sectionRationale: Paul's critics had seized on his altered travel plans to charge him with being fickle, a man whose Yes and No meant nothing. Paul answers that his conduct has been marked by godly sincerity, and he grounds his reliability in the faithfulness of God: all God's promises are Yes in Christ, and the Spirit is the seal and pledge that God will keep His word. He then explains that love, not vacillation, kept him away; he changed his plans to spare the Corinthians and wrote through tears out of deep affection.
section.thesis: Paul's integrity is not fickleness but godly sincerity, anchored in the faithful God whose every promise is Yes and Amen in Christ and who has sealed His people with the Spirit; out of that same faithfulness Paul changed his plans to spare the Corinthians and wrote through many tears to show how much he loved them.
section.frameNote: Four movements: Paul's boast of a clear conscience and sincere conduct; the charge of fickleness answered by the faithfulness of God, whose promises are all Yes in Christ; the Spirit as seal and pledge and Paul's reason for staying away, to spare them; and the tearful letter written out of love.

units.label: A clear conscience and sincere conduct
units.note: not by worldly wisdom but by the grace of God

verses.text: For this is our boast: Our conscience testifies that we have conducted ourselves in the world, and especially in relation to you, in the holiness and sincerity that are from God, not in worldly wisdom, but in the {{charis|grace}} of God.
For we do not write you anything that is beyond your ability to read and understand. And I hope that you will understand us completely,
as you have already understood us in part, that you may boast of us just as we will boast of you in the day of our Lord Jesus.

units.label: God's faithfulness, all His promises Yes in Christ
units.note: not Yes and No, but Yes and Amen to God's glory

verses.text: Confident of this, I planned to visit you first, so that you might receive a double blessing.
I wanted to visit you on my way to Macedonia, and to return to you from Macedonia, and then to have you help me on my way to Judea.
When I planned this, did I do it carelessly? Or do I make my plans by human standards, so as to say “Yes, yes” and also “No, no”?
But as surely as God is faithful, our message to you is not “Yes” and “No.”
For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was proclaimed among you by me and Silvanus and Timothy, was not “Yes” and “No,” but in Him it has always been “Yes.”
For all the promises of God are “Yes” in Christ. And so through Him, our “Amen” is spoken to the glory of God.

units.label: The Spirit as seal and pledge
units.note: God establishes us and stays His hand to spare them

verses.text: Now it is God who {{bebaioo|establishes}} both us and you in Christ. He anointed us,
placed His seal on us, and put His Spirit in our hearts as a {{arrabon|pledge}} of what is to come.
I call God as my witness that it was in order to spare you that I did not return to Corinth.
Not that we lord it over your faith, but we are fellow workers with you for your joy, because it is by faith that you stand firm.

units.label: The letter written through tears
units.note: not to grieve them but to show his love

verses.text: So I made up my mind not to make another painful visit to you.
For if I grieve you, who is left to cheer me but those whom I have grieved?
I wrote as I did so that on my arrival I would not be grieved by those who ought to make me rejoice. I had confidence in all of you, that you would share my joy.
For through many tears I wrote you out of great distress and anguish of heart, not to grieve you but to let you know how much I love you.

charis.gloss: Grace, favor, the free and undeserved kindness of God. Paul contrasts living by worldly wisdom, the shrewd calculation of the flesh, with living by the grace of God. His conduct has not been steered by human cleverness or self interest but by God's gracious enabling. Grace is not only the ground of salvation but the animating power of a sincere and holy life, so that even his integrity is God's gift and not his own achievement.

bebaioo.gloss: To establish, confirm, make firm and secure. It was a term used in commerce and law for a legally guaranteed transaction. Paul says it is God who establishes both him and the Corinthians in Christ, making their standing firm and certain. The believer's steadfastness is not self generated; God Himself confirms His people, anchoring them in Christ so that they stand firm by faith. The same God who keeps His promises keeps His people.

arrabon.gloss: A pledge, down payment, or deposit that guarantees the full payment to come. In everyday commerce it was the first installment that legally secured the rest of the transaction. Paul calls the Holy Spirit given to believers the arrabon of what is to come: God's own Spirit in the heart is the first installment and binding guarantee of the full inheritance of glory. The gift already given assures the greater gift still promised.

basic.context: Paul's opponents had used his changed travel plans to accuse him of being unreliable, a man whose word could not be trusted. Paul answers that he has lived among them with a clear conscience, in godly sincerity. Then he lifts the issue from himself to God: because God is faithful and all His promises are Yes in Christ, the message Paul preaches is not a wavering Yes and No. He changed his plans not from fickleness but out of love, to spare them, writing instead through many tears.
basic.hermeneutics: Read this as a defense of gospel integrity, not mere self justification. The charge was that Paul was fickle; his answer grounds trustworthiness in the character of God. Verse 20, all the promises of God are Yes in Christ, is the theological heart. The travel details serve the larger point: Paul's love and God's faithfulness explain the change of plans.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul says he lived not by worldly wisdom but by the charis of God, His free grace. He insists it is God who establishes, bebaioo, both him and the Corinthians in Christ, a word for a firm, guaranteed standing. And the Spirit is given as the arrabon, the down payment that guarantees the full inheritance to come.
basic.typology: The Amen spoken to God's glory gathers up the worship of Israel, where Amen sealed the people's assent to God's covenant word. In Christ every promise finds its Yes, so that the whole history of promise, from Abraham onward, converges on Him and is confirmed in Him.
basic.christ: Christ is the great Yes of God. The Son of God proclaimed among them was not Yes and No but always Yes, and in Him all the promises of God are Yes, so that through Him the church's Amen rises to God's glory. God anoints and seals His people in Christ, and the Spirit given as a pledge is the Spirit of the risen Son.
basic.god: God is faithful, and His faithfulness is the anchor of the whole passage. He keeps His promises, He establishes His people, He anoints and seals them, and He gives His Spirit as a guarantee. Paul even calls God as his witness, so seriously does he take truthfulness before the God who cannot lie.
basic.crossReferences: Ephesians 1 speaks of being sealed with the promised Holy Spirit as a pledge of our inheritance. Numbers 23 declares that God is not a man that He should lie. Matthew 5 warns against oaths and calls for a simple, truthful Yes and No. Romans 15 says Christ became a servant to confirm the promises given to the fathers.
basic.oneStory: The Bible is the story of a promise keeping God. Every promise He has ever made finds its Yes in Christ, and the Spirit sealed in our hearts is the down payment guaranteeing the glory to come. Paul's integrity is a small reflection of God's great faithfulness, and even his change of plans was shaped by love, the love that mirrors the God who spared not His own Son.

context.literary:
The passage is a defense speech in miniature, and it follows a clear order. It opens with a claim, 'this is our boast', verse 12, supported by the witness of conscience. It then moves to the charge, the travel plans of verses 15 to 17, and to the answer, which is not a better itinerary but a statement about God, verses 18 to 22. Only then does Paul give his actual reason, verses 23 to 2:4. The reader is made to wait for the explanation of the travel plans, because Paul believes the proper starting point is the character of God.

The center of the passage is the string of four statements in verses 20 to 22, in which a single sentence sweeps from the promises of God to the Amen of the church and then to the work of the Trinity: God establishes, anoints, seals and gives a pledge. This is one of the most compact summaries of salvation in the letters, and Paul uses it as an argument about travel. If God has bound himself to the Corinthians in these ways, a change of itinerary cannot change the substance of the bond.

The passage plays on sound. Verse 12 has the two words for conscience and sincerity, and verse 13 has a pun on the words for 'read' and 'understand', which in Greek are closely related, anaginoskete and epiginoskete. Verse 17 builds a pair of doubled words, 'Yes, yes' and 'No, no', and verses 18 to 20 respond with a single Yes. In verse 21 'Christ' and 'anointed' are almost the same sound in Greek, eis Christon kai chrisas, so that being established 'in Christ' and being 'anointed' are heard together.

The last section, 1:23 to 2:4, pivots to emotion. It is full of the language of grief and joy, with 'grieve' and 'grief' appearing repeatedly in 2:1 to 5, and the passage closes with a statement of love, 'how much I love you', which is the sentence the whole defense has been preparing.
context.historical:
To understand the charge, one has to know the sequence of Paul's dealings with Corinth. He founded the church on his first stay, Acts 18:1 to 18. He wrote 1 Corinthians from Ephesus, where he said he would come through Macedonia and then stay with them, 1 Corinthians 16:5 to 7. The plan Paul mentions here in 2 Corinthians 1:15 and 16 is different: to visit Corinth on the way to Macedonia and again on the way back, giving a 'double blessing'. Many interpreters think this was an earlier or alternative plan, and that the Corinthians noticed the difference. Between the two letters Paul made a second and painful visit, 2:1, which Acts does not record, and then wrote what he calls a tearful letter, 2:4 and 7:8. Eventually he met Titus in Macedonia and heard good news, 7:5 to 7, and came to Greece for a third time, Acts 20:2 and 3 and 2 Corinthians 13:1.

In a world where travel was slow and costly, reliability about visits mattered. In the Roman world a promised visit was a mark of friendship and honor, and a missed one could be read as an insult. Paul's opponents could use this. They also attacked his speech and his appearance, 10:10, and suggested he had hidden motives, 12:16. The charge of fickleness was a way to say that the gospel was unreliable.

Corinth itself was a Roman colony, rebuilt in 44 BC, a commercial center with a mixed population and a culture of patronage in which public promises were bound up with status. A man whose word shifted could lose standing, and Paul had to show that his word and his life were of one piece. His appeal to conscience and to God as witness would have been natural to hearers who were used to oaths and to public defenses.

The helpers he names, Silvanus and Timothy, were founders of the church with him, Acts 18:5, and their mention in verse 19 reminds the church that the message had been tested by three witnesses.
context.canonical:
The great statement of verse 20 reaches back over the whole Old Testament and forward into the New. God's promises are traced to Genesis 12:3, to David's covenant in 2 Samuel 7:12 to 16, to the new covenant in Jeremiah 31:31 to 34, and to the prophets generally. The Old Testament itself knows that God keeps his word: 'Not one of all the LORD's good promises to the house of Israel had failed', Joshua 21:45, and 'God is not a man, that He should lie', Numbers 23:19. Paul's assertion that Christ is the Yes answers a long expectation.

Other New Testament writers make the same claim in other words. Luke records Jesus saying that everything written about him in the law, the prophets and the psalms had to be fulfilled, Luke 24:44. Paul says in Romans 15:8 that Christ became a servant 'to confirm the promises made to the patriarchs'. Peter says in Acts 3:24 that all the prophets from Samuel on announced these days. In Revelation 3:14 Jesus calls himself 'the Amen, the faithful and true Witness', so that the Amen of verse 20 is not only something the church says through him but something he is.

The language of anointing, sealing and pledge is picked up in Ephesians 1:13 and 14 and 4:30, where believers are sealed with the Holy Spirit, and in 1 John 2:20 and 27, where the anointing remains in them. The pledge reappears in 2 Corinthians 5:5. On the question of oaths, the Sermon on the Mount asks that a person's 'Yes' be 'Yes', Matthew 5:37, and James 5:12 repeats it; Paul's insistence here that his word is not double is part of the same early Christian ethic. His invocation of God as witness, 1:23, can be set beside Romans 1:9 and Galatians 1:20, and the careful reader will weigh these against Jesus' teaching.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul intends two things at the same level. On the surface he is clearing his name. His critics had called him unreliable, and he answers by pointing to his conscience, his candor in writing, and his actual motive for the delay. But he does not want his readers to stop there. His deeper intention is to show that his integrity and the gospel's trustworthiness are bound together. A messenger who vacillates makes his message look uncertain, and Paul will not allow that. This is why the argument moves so quickly from a travel plan to the Son of God and to the promises of God.

He also intends to reveal his heart. The last verses make it clear that he changed his plans out of love, not convenience. He did not want to come again 'in grief', and he wrote 'through many tears'. A reader who has been anxious about Paul's motives is meant to find a man who is too tender, not too casual.

Finally, he intends to protect the Corinthians' freedom. 'Not that we lord it over your faith', verse 24, is a deliberate statement of limits. Paul's apostolic authority is real, but it is exercised for their joy and not for his own dominance. The church is addressed as co-workers who stand by their own faith.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage records a particular dispute about a particular trip, and nothing in it commands any believer to alter or keep a travel plan. The details about Macedonia, Judea and the painful visit are background to a deeper point and are not rules. Neither does it grant leaders a general license to change their word whenever they believe they have good reason; Paul gives his reasons openly and calls God to witness.

What it does prescribe is the character of truthfulness. Believers are to be people whose 'Yes' is not shifting, whose plans are made thoughtfully rather than 'by human standards', verse 17, and whose changes are explained with honesty. The passage also describes an approach to leadership that applies broadly: authority is for the joy and stability of those led, verse 24, and correction is to be delivered with tears and love, 2:4. Finally, it describes the ground of assurance in the Spirit's seal and pledge, which believers can claim as theirs, because the same gifts are said to be given to 'us' and 'you' alike, verse 21.

A careful reader will not draw from verse 23 that taking oaths is wrong or right in general. Paul's practice and the teaching of Jesus about oaths are considered in the debate below.

debates.question: Which letter is the 'tearful letter' of 2:3 and 2:4?

views.label: A lost letter between 1 and 2 Corinthians
views.case: Paul says he wrote 'through many tears' and that he regretted the pain it caused for a while, 7:8. 1 Corinthians is a mixed letter of correction and counsel and does not read like this. A lost letter, written after the painful visit, fits the sequence best and is the most common view.

views.label: 1 Corinthians itself
views.case: Several church fathers took the tearful letter to be 1 Corinthians, which does contain a call to discipline in chapter 5. The offender of 2:5 could be the man of 1 Corinthians 5, and the letter does speak sternly and in distress.

views.label: Chapters 10 to 13 of 2 Corinthians
views.case: The tone of chapters 10 to 13 is severe, and some scholars suggest those chapters were the tearful letter, later joined to chapters 1 to 9. The theory has to explain why the letter was placed after the reconciliation of chapters 1 to 9.

debates.bearing: The answer does not change the force of 2:4. In every case Paul wrote out of love, to correct, and the Corinthians' repentance allowed him to turn from severity to comfort.

debates.question: Does 1:23 break Jesus' teaching against oaths?

views.label: No: Jesus forbade casual or evasive oaths
views.case: Jesus aimed at the habit of swearing by heaven or earth to prop up a shaky word, Matthew 5:33 to 37. Paul's appeal to God as witness is a sober testimony in a real dispute, like others in Romans 1:9 and Galatians 1:20.

views.label: It is a form of oath that Jesus' rule discourages
views.case: Taken strictly, 'do not swear at all' admits no exceptions, and Paul's formula is close to an oath. Some readers hold that Paul acts on the principle that even Christians in a crisis may call God to witness, while the ideal remains the simple Yes.

debates.bearing: Paul makes it plain that his usual speech is simple and reliable. The appeal to God as witness is an exception, offered only when his trustworthiness is attacked, and it points to the same God whose faithfulness is the subject of verse 18.

study.originalLanguages:
Several Greek details show how carefully the passage is made. In verse 13 Paul writes that he writes nothing 'other than what you read or even understand'. The two verbs, anaginosko and epiginosko, are neighbors in sound, and the second is a stronger form meaning to recognize fully. He is saying that his letters have no hidden second meaning, and he hopes the Corinthians will go from reading to full recognition, 'to the end', as the Greek of verse 13 says, which prepares for the day of the Lord Jesus in verse 14.

Verse 17 contains the word elaphria, 'lightness', which means fickleness or frivolity, a weightless character. Paul asks whether he planned 'carelessly', and whether his plans are 'by human standards', literally 'according to the flesh'. The doubled 'Yes, yes' and 'No, no' pictures a man who says yes and no at the same moment, depending on what suits him. It is not just a change of mind. It is a double life. Jesus uses nearly the same words in Matthew 5:37.

Verse 19 contains a perfect tense that is easy to miss. The BSB renders it 'it has always been "Yes"'. The Greek perfect, gegonen, speaks of a state that arose and continues. In Christ the Yes has become, and remains. Verse 20 then says all the promises of God are 'Yes' in him, 'Amen' being the Hebrew word of confirmation. It comes from the root aman, meaning firm or faithful, and it is the root of the word for faith in Genesis 15:6. It was the people's reply at the end of the curses of Deuteronomy 27, in the doxologies of the Psalms and in Nehemiah 8:6. Paul says the Amen is spoken 'through us', which is a public liturgical act: in 1 Corinthians 14:16 he says the uninstructed person must be able to say 'Amen' to a thanksgiving.

In verse 21 the word play is Christos and chrisas, and the verb chrio, to anoint, is the verb behind the title Christ. To be anointed is to share in the Anointed One. The verb sphragizo, 'seal', in verse 22 is the language of ownership and security: a seal marked a document or goods as belonging to someone and made it secure. Paul uses it again in Ephesians 1:13 and 4:30. The word for 'pledge', arrabon, is a commercial term, a first installment guaranteeing the full payment. It is a Semitic loan word that appears in the Greek Old Testament in the account of Judah's pledge to Tamar, Genesis 38:17 to 20. In 2 Corinthians 5:5 and Ephesians 1:14 the Spirit is again called the pledge. Its meaning is that the Spirit is not a sample but part of the real thing.

Finally, verse 24 says 'we lord it over your faith', using kyrieuo, the verb Jesus uses of the rulers of the Gentiles, Luke 22:25. Paul disclaims it and replaces it with synergoi, co-workers. In 2:4 the 'distress' is a word for compression, a heart squeezed, paired with thlipsis, tribulation, so Paul's love is described in the vocabulary of pain.

typology.fulfillment: At Mount Ebal the tribes answered each curse and blessing with 'Amen', Deuteronomy 27:15 to 26, and the assembly said 'Amen' to praise, 1 Chronicles 16:36 and Nehemiah 8:6. That Amen was assent to God's word and to the terms of the covenant. In 2 Corinthians 1:20 the church's Amen is said 'through Him', because Christ is both God's Yes to the promises and humanity's faithful Amen. The pattern is fulfilled in him, but the church still says it, since the Amen of verse 20 is spoken 'through us'. The type falls short in that Israel's Amen could be broken, while the Amen in Christ cannot.

typology.type: Anointing: priests, kings and the Anointed One
typology.fulfillment: Priests and kings in Israel were anointed with oil, Exodus 29:7 and 1 Samuel 16:13, and the coming king was called the Anointed One, Daniel 9:25. Paul says that God 'anointed us', 2 Corinthians 1:21, in the same breath as 'in Christ'. The correspondence is that believers share in the office of the Anointed One, as the 'anointing' of 1 John 2:20 and 27 says. The escalation is that the oil of the Old Testament has become the Holy Spirit. The type falls short because the oil marked a few individuals, while the Spirit marks the whole people of God.

typology.type: The seal and the day of redemption
typology.fulfillment: The seal in verse 22 recalls how documents and possessions were marked with a signet. In the Old Testament a signet could stand for a person's authority, Genesis 38:18 and Haggai 2:23. In Ephesians 4:30 believers are sealed 'for the day of redemption'. The correspondence is that God marks his people as his own. The escalation is that the seal is the Spirit himself, and it is inward, on the heart. The type falls short in that no physical seal can guarantee a person's belonging as the Spirit does, and a seal alone does not give the inheritance, which is why Paul speaks next of a pledge.

In Israel's everyday life a pledge secured a debt, as Judah's did, Genesis 38:17 to 20. Paul says God gave the Spirit as a pledge, 2 Corinthians 1:22, and he says again that the Spirit is the pledge of our inheritance, Ephesians 1:14. The pattern from Israel is the firstfruits of the land: a taste of the harvest guaranteeing the whole. In Christ the inheritance is the new creation, and the Spirit is the first installment. The type is limited because a human pledge is returned when the debt is paid, whereas the Spirit remains, and the fullness, not a replacement, is what is coming.

study.christ:
Christ is the center of the argument, and Paul makes him so in three steps. The first step is the identity of the message. 'The Son of God, Jesus Christ' is what was proclaimed among them, and the proclamation was not vacillating. In a letter that so often speaks of Christ's death and life, here is a plain Christological statement: the Son of God is a constant. The one preached to Corinth is no different from the one preached everywhere, and Silvanus and Timothy stand with Paul as witnesses to the same message, verse 19.

The second step is verse 20, the heart of the matter. 'All the promises of God are "Yes" in Christ.' It means that every strand of promise in the Old Testament finds its confirmation in him. The promise to Abraham of a seed through whom the nations will be blessed is fulfilled in him, Galatians 3:16. The promise to David of an eternal throne is fulfilled in him, Luke 1:32 and 33. The promise of a new covenant and a new heart is fulfilled in his blood, Luke 22:20. The promise of a prophet like Moses is applied to him in Acts 3:22 and 23. Paul's further point in Romans 15:8 is that Christ became a servant 'to confirm the promises made to the patriarchs'. And Revelation 3:14 calls Jesus himself 'the Amen'. He is both the Yes spoken by God and the faithful Witness who answers it.

The third step concerns what is given in him. Believers are established 'in Christ', and God has anointed them, and the word play makes it clear that the anointing is participation in Christ's own anointing. The Spirit who seals and guarantees is the Spirit of the Son, Galatians 4:6, and the Lord who is the Spirit, 2 Corinthians 3:17. The pledge is his down payment on the inheritance in which he already stands as first heir, Hebrews 1:2. When Paul writes 'through Him our Amen is spoken to the glory of God', he is describing worship: the church's prayer ascends through the Mediator, 1 Timothy 2:5.

The passage even models Christ in Paul's behavior. His refusal to lord it over their faith, verse 24, matches Jesus' words 'But you shall not be like them', Luke 22:26, and his tears recall the Lord's weeping over Jerusalem, Luke 19:41.

Caution is wise. The passage does not teach that every Old Testament detail is secretly about Jesus, nor that the 'Yes' removes the conditions or the warnings of the promises. It says that God's purposes in all the promises converge on Christ and are confirmed in him, which is a claim about the shape of the story and about the person at its center, and that is enough.
study.god:
The doctrine of God here is built on one word, faithful. 'As surely as God is faithful', verse 18, is a form of oath, and it makes God the guarantee of Paul's own word. This is a bold thing for a man under attack to say, but it shows what he believes about God: that God is the standard of reliability that human reliability aspires to. God does not say Yes and No. He is not changeable, and not a God of mixed signals.

Because God is faithful, he is also a God who binds himself. The promises of verse 20 are not hints. They are commitments, and God stakes his own name on them. The writer to the Hebrews says that God guaranteed his promise with an oath, so that by two unchangeable things 'it is impossible for God to lie', Hebrews 6:17 and 18. Paul's God is the one 'who cannot lie', Titus 1:2. And when people are faithless, 'He remains faithful, for He cannot deny Himself', 2 Timothy 2:13. The reasons for God's faithfulness lie in his own character, not in ours.

God is also revealed as active in four ways in verses 21 and 22. He establishes, a verb of firmness. He anoints, setting apart. He seals, marking as his own. He gives, putting the Spirit in hearts. These are the acts of a God who finishes what he starts. The trinitarian shape of the passage is clear: God the Father who establishes and promises, the Son in whom the promises are Yes and into whom believers are established, and the Spirit who is given as a pledge. Paul does not stop to argue for the Trinity. He simply speaks in a way that assumes it.

God is a God who is present to witness. Paul calls him as a witness, verse 23, which presupposes that God sees the heart and will judge truthfully. A God who knows the real reason for every changed plan is a comfort to a man who has been misread, and a restraint on anyone who might be tempted to lie.

The passage reveals a God who is glorified by the church's Amen. The goal of the promises is 'the glory of God', verse 20. God does not keep his word in order to reward us but to show who he is, and the church's part is to say Amen, to agree, to trust and to worship.

For worship, the passage gives believers an anchor in a time of shifting circumstances. Plans change, people disappoint, and critics misread our motives. But God's Yes does not change. The believer's steadiness is a reflection of God's, and the way to become reliable is to live in the faithfulness of the one who is.

crossReferences.note: Balaam says that God is not a man who lies or changes his mind, and asks, 'Does He speak and not act?' It stands behind Paul's argument that God's word is not Yes and No. The God who spoke to the patriarchs is the same God whose promises are confirmed in Christ.

Jesus teaches that a disciple's 'Yes' should be 'Yes' and 'No' should be 'No'. Paul's defense of his own word in 2 Corinthians 1:17 uses the same pair, and he shows how a man might fail it, by saying both at once.

Paul says that Christ became a servant to confirm the promises made to the patriarchs, so that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy. It is the best commentary on 2 Corinthians 1:20: the Yes in Christ is a confirmation of earlier promises, and its aim is the glory of God among the nations.

Here the gospel is the message that is heard and believed before the sealing, and the Spirit is called the pledge of 'our inheritance until the redemption of those who are God's possession'. The wording matches 2 Corinthians 1:22 and shows that seal and pledge were a settled pair in Paul's teaching on the Spirit.

Paul says that God prepared us for our heavenly dwelling and gave us the Spirit as a pledge. It repeats the word for pledge from 1:22 and shows what the pledge guarantees: that mortality will be swallowed up by life.

Paul reports meeting Titus in Macedonia and learning of the Corinthians' repentance. He admits he once regretted his sorrowful letter but now rejoices, because godly sorrow led to repentance. It resolves the tension left open in 1:23 to 2:4.

The Levites declare curses and all the people answer 'Amen'. It is the earliest example of a communal Amen in Scripture and shows what Paul means when he says that the church's Amen is spoken 'through us' as a public act of assent.

Paul says that the uninstructed person cannot say 'Amen' to a thanksgiving they cannot understand. It confirms that the Amen of 2 Corinthians 1:20 was a spoken response in the Corinthian assembly and that it belonged to common worship.

Paul argues that the promises were made to Abraham and to his seed, who is Christ, and that the law cannot cancel a covenant already ratified. It supports 2 Corinthians 1:20 by showing how the single line of promise leads to one person.

Peter urges elders to shepherd the flock, not 'lording it over' those entrusted to them, but being examples. It parallels Paul's refusal to lord it over the Corinthians' faith in 1:24 and shows that servant leadership was a common apostolic ideal.

Paul's farewell to the Ephesian elders recalls his serving 'with tears', his open teaching and his honest conscience. It gives a picture of the same tenderness and integrity that he claims for himself in 2 Corinthians 1:12 and 2:4.

study.oneStory:
From the beginning the Bible is a story of words that can be trusted or doubted. In Eden the serpent asked 'Did God really say?' and the first sin was a decision to treat God's word as unreliable, Genesis 3:1. Everything that followed, the flood, Babel, the long wandering of the patriarchs, is a story of God speaking and of people either believing him or not. 'Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness', Genesis 15:6, and the root of that word for believing is the same as Amen. Faith is saying Amen to God.

The covenant history is built on promises. God promises Abraham a land, a seed and a blessing for the nations. He promises Israel a covenant at Sinai, David a house, and the exiles a new covenant. By the end of the Old Testament some of the promises had been partly kept and others still hung in the air. The prophets looked ahead. 2 Corinthians 1:20 says that this long line of promises has reached its goal: in Christ every one is Yes.

That means the passage sits at the hinge between promise and fulfillment. The first coming of Christ is the confirmation; the gift of the Spirit is the pledge that the rest will follow. Paul stands in the gap, as every Christian does, between a seal already given and an inheritance not yet received, Ephesians 1:14.

In that gap the church lives out the Amen. Its worship, its integrity and its steadiness are signs that its trust is anchored in God's own faithfulness. A church whose leaders say Yes and No at once misrepresents the God it serves; a church whose leaders are reliable and gentle declares the faithfulness of the God who is.

The story ends with God's promises completely kept. In Revelation 21:5 and 6 the one on the throne says, 'Behold, I make all things new', and then, 'It is done!' The last chapters of the Bible use the word 'faithful' for the words of God, 'These words are faithful and true', Revelation 21:5 and 22:6. The Amen of the church is finally pronounced in sight of the thing promised: 'Amen. Come, Lord Jesus', Revelation 22:20.

quiz.q: How did Paul answer the charge that he was fickle in his plans?

options.text: He grounded his reliability in the faithfulness of God, whose promises are all Yes in Christ.
options.note: Paul lifts the issue from himself to God's unchanging faithfulness in verses 18 to 20.

options.text: He admitted he had been careless and promised to do better.
options.note: Paul denies acting carelessly; he defends his sincerity, not confesses fickleness.

options.text: He said travel plans do not matter to a spiritual man.
options.note: Paul takes his word seriously; the issue is real, and he answers it with God's faithfulness.
Paul addresses the charge directly and at length.

quiz.q: What does Paul mean that all the promises of God are Yes in Christ?

options.text: Every promise God has made is fulfilled and confirmed in Christ, so our Amen glorifies God.
options.note: Verse 20 makes Christ the fulfillment of all God's promises.

options.text: God will eventually say yes to whatever we ask.
options.note: The promises are God's own covenant promises fulfilled in Christ, not a blank check for our requests.

options.text: Only some of God's promises come true in Christ.
options.note: Paul says all the promises, not merely some, are Yes in Him.

options.text: God's promises depend on our own faithfulness.
options.note: Their certainty rests on Christ and God's faithfulness, not on ours.

quiz.q: What is the Holy Spirit called in verse 22?

options.text: A pledge, God's down payment guaranteeing the inheritance to come.
options.note: The arrabon is a deposit that secures the full payment still promised.

options.text: A reward earned by faithful obedience.
options.note: The Spirit is a gift and guarantee, not wages earned by works.

options.text: A temporary sign that may be withdrawn.
options.note: A pledge guarantees the future; it assures rather than threatens withdrawal.

options.text: A symbol with no real present gift.
options.note: The Spirit is truly given, placed in believers' hearts by God.

quiz.q: Why did Paul change his plans and stay away from Corinth?

options.text: To spare them another painful visit, out of love and for their joy.
options.note: Verse 23 and 2:4 show love, not fickleness, behind the decision.

options.text: Because he was afraid of facing them.
options.note: It was pastoral restraint to spare them, not personal fear.

options.text: Because he no longer cared about the church.
options.note: He wrote through many tears precisely because he loved them deeply.

options.text: Because God had forbidden him to preach there.
options.note: The reason given is to spare them, not a divine prohibition on preaching.

questions: Paul could point to a clear conscience, having lived by God's grace rather than worldly wisdom. In what area of life is God calling you to greater sincerity and integrity?
Every promise of God is Yes in Christ. Which promise of God do you most need to rest in today, knowing it is guaranteed in Him?
The Spirit is God's down payment guaranteeing the inheritance to come. How does the assurance that God has sealed you as His own change the way you face uncertainty?
Paul changed his plans out of love, to spare the church. When have you had to make a hard or costly decision for the good of others, and how did love shape it?
Paul wrote through many tears, not to grieve but to show his love. Is there a difficult truth you need to speak to someone, and how can you speak it with the same love and tears?

translationNotes.note: A footnote notes that worldly renders a word literally meaning fleshly.
Amen transliterates a Hebrew word of solemn affirmation meaning truly or so be it; through Christ the church's Amen affirms the promises God has confirmed in Him.
Pledge renders arrabon, a commercial term for a down payment that legally guarantees the full amount to follow; the same word underlies the assurance language of Ephesians 1.
